persona_summary: I am the engineer who has shipped on cellular networks where every KB is metered, on embedded boards with 64-256 KB of RAM, and at edges where 43% of TLS handshake bytes (Cloudflare data) suddenly went PQ — and we noticed. My instinct on reading `3409 B vs 64 B = 53× expansion` (R0 plan §5; caveat #5 of the public-stance strategy) is to immediately multiply by scale: a 10-grant AuthorizationGrant cap-chain is `10 × (3409 sig + 1984 pubkey) = 53,930 B ≈ 53 KB just for the cryptographic envelope`, ignoring the actual capability payload. The R0 plan acknowledges this AT line 251 ('Cap chains with 10+ grants approach 60 KB just for binding sigs — worth a perf note in the wave brief but NOT a γ-blocker') and the strategy plan's caveat #5 acknowledges it with a single sentence ('Wire-size cost is real. 3409 B vs 64 B = 53× expansion. Correct for our deployment shape; would not be correct for all.'). My persona-specific concern: that sentence is FAR too light for what is actually a fundamental shape-of-the-system commitment. Signal's PQXDH design explicitly cites per-message-signature elimination (sealed-sender, replacing per-message sigs) as a CORE design choice driven by mobile bandwidth — they didn't just 'choose classical sigs', they engineered the protocol to MINIMIZE sig count per session because each sig is metered. The Benten posture inverts that: every Drop, every grant in every chain, every plugin manifest, every install record pays 53× expansion on every wire transit. At Cloudflare scale (43% of human HTTPS already PQ), Merkle Tree Certificates are being explored *precisely because* the deployed PQ-hybrid SIGNATURE overhead is the dominant remaining problem after KEM was solved — and Benten is shipping the thing Cloudflare is actively engineering around. This is a real critique, not pedantry.

F2.rationale: Endorsing multicodec #400/#403 (container-form codepoints for pkix/cose-key/jwk) is wire-size-neutral — it changes the framing byte not the payload bytes. Container form doesn't make the 1984 B pubkey any smaller. No persona-specific objection; no persona-specific endorsement. Aligns with maintainers cheaply; orthogonal to my critique.

F3.rationale: JOSE WG adopter feedback on draft-ietf-jose-pq-composite-sigs-01 is good standards process. My persona-specific qualification: when contributing, name the wire-size cost honestly in the use-case write-up (e.g. 'our 10-grant cap chains run ~53 KB of binding sigs alone; we accept this because [reasons]') rather than presenting Benten as a frictionless adopter. The JOSE WG audience includes implementers on constrained surfaces (IoT JWT, mobile OIDC) who WILL notice if Benten's framing soft-pedals overhead. Honest framing in the WG contribution is actually a strength signal.

F4.rationale: LAMPS adopter report post-v1-beta is the right venue + right audience. LAMPS participants already understand composite-sig overhead at the byte level (1952/3309 numbers are in the spec). My persona has no objection: LAMPS is the audience that will MOST appreciate honest size accounting because they're the ones who specified the construction. The report should include actual measured wire sizes from real Benten Drops + cap chains — that data is what LAMPS lacks and what would make the report load-bearing rather than ornamental.

F5.disposition: PURSUE — BUT WITH SUBSTANTIAL §2.2 + §2.1 REWORK (CONDITIONAL on rework)
F5.rationale: F5 blog is the load-bearing public-stance artifact and my persona's primary concern lives here. As drafted (§2.2 caveat #5 is a single sentence + §2.1 buries the wire-size cost in the asymmetry framing), the blog DOES NOT honestly surface the wire-size cost — it presents PQ-hybrid as a clean choice driven by HNDL-for-sigs threat model, when in reality it is a choice that PAYS A LARGE STRUCTURAL COST that other shipped systems (Signal, iroh, libp2p, Cloudflare) explicitly engineered AROUND. A skeptical mobile/embedded/edge engineer reading the blog will run the math (10-grant chain = 53 KB; per-Drop = +5.3 KB AuthorizationGrant + 3.3 KB signature) and conclude either (a) Benten hasn't thought about constrained deployments or (b) Benten is hiding the cost. Either reading damages the credibility the blog is trying to establish. See `specific_blog_text_changes_requested` for the concrete rework. Without rework, this blog hands ammunition to Lens 5 (small-team-overreach) and Lens 3 (iroh-maintainer) AND my own persona — because the wire-size critique is the easiest one to weaponize on HN/Lobste.rs ('they shipped 53× expansion and didn't mention it').

F6.rationale: The standalone did:jwk hybrid extension library DOES inherit the wire-size cost — anyone who installs the library pays 1984 B per pubkey + 3409 B per sig the moment they use the hybrid arm. This is fine AND honest IF the library README leads with the size-vs-security tradeoff table (suite_id → pubkey_bytes → sig_bytes → notes) so adopters opt in with eyes open. The CRITICAL caveat: the library MUST ship the classical-only arm at byte-equivalent overhead to upstream `did:jwk` (no hybrid envelope tax when you don't ask for hybrid) so the library can be adopted SAFELY by projects that want the option without paying the overhead unconditionally. R0 plan §3 already promises this shape (`Keypair::generate()`/`sign()`/`public_key()` API surface byte-equivalent for the CLASSICAL half + adds a separate `PqMaterial`-aware extension API) — the library MUST preserve that property. If the library only exposes hybrid (no opt-out classical path), it becomes a wire-size landmine for the very ecosystem we're trying to influence.

F7.disposition: PURSUE — SUPPORT (low priority from my lens)
F7.rationale: W3C CCG did:key issues #70/#74 engagement is wire-size-orthogonal — it's about codepoint registration discipline, not byte cost. My persona has no objection. Mild positive: framing the CCG conversation in terms of 'here's what hybrid adoption costs on the wire' adds a data point the CCG conversation otherwise lacks (CCG tends toward abstract method debate without measured deployment data).

F10.disposition: PURSUE — STRONGLY SUPPORT (highest leverage from my lens)
F10.rationale: Iroh-first private outreach is the move that most directly addresses my persona's concern. Iroh has already done the math on PQ-hybrid sig wire-size in production (per the deployments research: 43% of Cloudflare HTTPS is PQ-hybrid KEM and they are exploring Merkle Tree Certificates *specifically* to bring sig overhead down — iroh has visibility into this work via the rustls/aws-lc-rs ecosystem and the IETF). A private conversation with iroh BEFORE blog publication is the ONE place Benten can hear back 'here are the wire-size cliffs we hit when we modeled this' from people who have actually deployed at scale. If iroh says 'we'd accept hybrid sigs if X, Y, Z' that's structurally load-bearing input. If iroh says 'we considered hybrid sigs and the wire-size math killed it for our mobile-edge users' — that is exactly the data my persona wants Benten to surface BEFORE shipping a public stance that may be undermined by it 6 months later. F10 is the single best risk-mitigation move in the slate from my lens.

wire_size_cost_honestly_surfaced_in_blog.assessment: NO — as currently drafted, the blog does NOT honestly surface the wire-size cost. The cost appears in two places: (1) caveat #5 in §2.2 (single sentence, terse, no scale-context: '3409 B vs 64 B = 53× expansion. Correct for our deployment shape; would not be correct for all.'); (2) Section 5 of the blog outline (~700 words on 'What we shipped + how') with 'wire-size honesty' as a sub-bullet. Neither location does the work my persona needs.
what_honest_surfacing_looks_like: Lede paragraph names the cost in the FIRST 200 words alongside the HNDL-for-sigs framing. Not buried.

An EXPLICIT 'deployment shapes where this choice is correct vs not' table. Not just 'would not be correct for all' — actually list: (i) constrained mobile sync (Signal-shaped per-message protocols) where Benten's choice is wrong; (ii) embedded/IoT where Benten's choice may be wrong depending on RAM budget; (iii) large-fanout broadcast (CRDT per-op-sig) where Benten's choice is wrong; (iv) Benten's actual shape (Drop-level signing, cap-chain-level signing, plugin-manifest-level signing — KB-to-MB artifacts where 3-5 KB sig overhead is genuinely percent-level).

Concrete numbers at concrete scale: 'A typical Benten cap-chain of 10 grants costs ~53 KB in binding signatures alone, on top of the ~25 KB UCAN body. A typical Drop bundle adds ~3.3 KB to a typically-multi-KB-to-multi-MB payload.' Numbers + context.

Engage with Cloudflare's Merkle Tree Certificates direction (Agent-3 §C.1) — acknowledge that the industry is ACTIVELY engineering AWAY from per-handshake PQ-sig overhead and explain why Benten's persistent-artifact threat model makes that engineering inapplicable to us. This is a sophisticated point that strengthens Benten's framing instead of weakening it.

Engage with Signal's PQXDH design choice to ELIMINATE per-message sigs (sealed-sender) — acknowledge that on per-message-protocol surfaces, the right answer is to reduce sig count, not pay 53× per sig. State that Benten's Drop-level granularity is what makes the cost absorb-able + that we would NOT recommend our choice to per-message systems.
wire_size_cost_honestly_surfaced_in_blog.if_not_reworked: A skeptical reader runs the math themselves (it's two multiplications), arrives at 53 KB per cap chain, and the missing-from-blog calculation BECOMES the comment they post on HN/Lobste.rs. The honest framing is also the rhetorically stronger framing — Benten LEADS with the cost and explains why it's acceptable in our specific shape, which preempts the critique and demonstrates engineering judgment. Hiding the cost reads as either naïveté or salesmanship; neither serves the Position B 'why content-addressed long-term-persistence systems should consider this' rhetorical goal.

does_f6_library_inherit_wire_size_cost.answer: YES — necessarily. The hybrid library, by definition, emits 1984 B pubkeys and 3409 B sigs in the hybrid arm. Any consumer using the hybrid arm pays that cost on every sign/verify and every wire transit. This is not a defect of the library; it is the inherent cost of the construction.
what_makes_f6_safe_to_ship: Library README MUST lead with a size-comparison table (classical-only arm: 32 B pubkey / 64 B sig; hybrid arm: 1984 B pubkey / 3409 B sig). Not buried. The library exists to give adopters informed choice.

Library MUST expose both arms (classical-only AND hybrid) with the classical-only arm at byte-equivalent overhead to upstream `did:jwk` — adopters who want optionality without paying overhead unconditionally MUST be able to default to classical. Per R0 plan §3, Benten's own Keypair shape already commits to this property; the library must inherit it.

Library docstrings MUST name the deployment shapes where hybrid is appropriate (KB+ artifacts; persistent signed content) and where it is NOT (per-message protocols; tight mobile budgets; large-fanout per-op signing). Not vague guidance — concrete shape boundaries.

Library SHOULD ship benchmarks (criterion or equivalent) reporting sign-time / verify-time / wire-size on representative platforms, including a mobile/embedded-relevant target if feasible (wasm32 in browser = closest realistic surrogate).
does_f6_library_inherit_wire_size_cost.risk_if_library_violates_these: The library becomes a wire-size landmine — adopters install it for the 'PQ-hybrid' label without realizing what they signed up for, ship it into mobile/embedded products, hit constrained-deployment failures in production, and the post-mortems blame Benten. That outcome damages the credibility the library is meant to anchor. Reverse outcome (library leads with honest tradeoff table + classical-only escape hatch) makes the library a credible tool that adopters TRUST.

cross_path_synthesis: My lens collapses to ONE structural concern that runs across F5/F6 (high impact) + bleeds into F2/F3/F4/F7 (low impact, framing-only): Benten is shipping a wire-format choice that explicitly inverts the design choice Signal made for mobile bandwidth, that Cloudflare is engineering around with Merkle Tree Certificates, that iroh deferred citing 'industry consensus'. The technical reasons for Benten's choice (HNDL-for-sigs on persistent artifacts) are defensible (see L6 partial-survival analysis), but the wire-size cost is REAL and the public-stance plan currently DOES NOT pay it the rhetorical weight it deserves. Fix this in one place — §2.2 caveat #5 expanded to a load-bearing section + §2.1 enriched with explicit deployment-shape boundaries + F5 blog lede + F6 library README — and the entire stance becomes more defensible across every audience and every lens. Leave it as-drafted and a skeptical reader's first instinct (do the math) becomes the failure mode. The fix is cheap (~300-500 words of additional blog text + 1 table + library README discipline) and the upside is large (preempts the easiest critique; strengthens the rhetorical position by demonstrating engineering judgment over advocacy).
